item.title: Meditations on Moloch
item.description: Scott Alexander · Why now: pacing the frontier is a textbook Moloch problem. Every lab says it wants to slow down, and none can safely do it alone. This essay is where the community's word for that trap comes from, and people will say 'Moloch' to you assuming you've read it. It's also some of the best prose the rationalist world has produced.

item.description: Jeremy Avigad · Avigad, a CMU logician and formal-proof pioneer, argues that now that AI handles yesterday's publishable problems, mathematicians should chase harder, more conceptual questions and treat proof assistants and neural nets as real mathematical tools. item.description: William P. Thurston · Why now: Harlev's argument today, that AI-proven results without human understanding shouldn't earn credit, is Thurston's argument from thirty years ago. item.title: Vallentin: why he became a mathematician, and why he still would
item.description: Proofs and Prompts · Frank Vallentin, a professor at the University of Cologne, traces his path from teenage programming to mathematics. He sees superhuman AI provers as the fulfillment of his teenage dream of automating mathematics, not a threat. item.title: Evidence about risk should be transparent
item.description: Ajeya Cotra · Cotra argues that third-party safety work should produce and publish raw evidence about loss-of-control risk instead of only certifying labs' claims. "The science on loss-of-control risk is, to put it generously, nascent." If you lean empirical, this lays out an open-science research agenda you could join.

item.title: Politics and the English Language
item.description: George Orwell · Why now: the government is renaming 'artificial intelligence' to 'super intelligence' on official documents, and every side of the AI debate is fighting over words ('pace', 'pause', 'hoax'). This is the essay on how political language works, and a model of plain prose. The six rules at the end are worth keeping.

item.title: We Must Pace the Frontier
item.description: Dario Amodei · The document the whole month is arguing about. Amodei proposes three steps to slow how fast frontier capabilities grow: embedded outside evaluators (Anthropic has committed to this unilaterally), coordination among labs in democratic countries, and global coordination. OpenAI adopted step one today. Read the original before the commentary.
